analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to publicly report how many claims they deny and why.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with no cosponsors and was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directs the Labor Department to write a rule requiring employer group health plans to report, in their annual federal filings, detailed data on claim denials: how many claims were submitted, approved, denied, and appealed, how many denials were reversed on appeal, the reasons for denials (such as medical necessity or missing prior authorization), dollar amounts denied, late decisions, and how many claims were decided by artificial intelligence. Plans would report these figures broken out for urgent care, inpatient, outpatient, prescription drug, mental health, and cancer-treatment claims [S2]. The bill does not ban any denial practice; it makes the denial data visible to regulators and the public [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People covered by employer health plans benefit from seeing, in one public place, how often their plan denies claims, why, and how often denials fall apart on appeal. Regulators and journalists could use the data to spot plans that deny care at unusual rates or lean on automated tools, and patients deciding between plans would have denial rates available for the first time [S2]. Workers whose plans were previously exempt from detailed annual reporting because they are small would also be covered under the bill's provisions extending reporting duties to plans with fewer than 100 participants [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees covered by employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must report counts of claims submitted, approved, denied, and appealed, plus how many denials were reversed in whole or in part during appeals [S2].
Plans must report the reasons for denials, broken into categories such as medical necessity, lack of referral, lack of prior authorization, services excluded, and administrative reasons [S2].
Plans must report how many claims were processed using artificial intelligence or other automated decision-making tools, and how many of those were paid versus denied [S2].

Plans must report claims broken out by category: pre-service, post-service, urgent care, inpatient, outpatient, prescription drugs, mental health and substance use benefits, and cancer diagnosis and treatment [S2].
Plans must report total dollar amounts of claims paid and claims denied, plus how many claims missed the plan's own required decision deadlines [S2].
The bill extends the reporting requirement to plans with fewer than 100 participants, which are currently allowed a simplified form of annual reporting [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and the insurers or administrators that run their health plans would bear the cost of collecting, verifying, and reporting this data each year, a cost that is modest for large plans but heavier for small ones. Plans with 20 or fewer claims in a category are excused from reporting that category's breakdown, which softens the burden on the smallest plans [S2]. Some compliance cost could eventually be passed to workers through premiums, and plans would have their denial behavior exposed to public scrutiny for the first time.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires reporting only; it does not lower denial rates, ban AI-driven denials, or change any claim rules. A plan could report a high denial rate year after year and face no consequence under this law [S2].

The reporting is added to annual ERISA filings, which are not designed for easy public reading; consumers may not actually see or use the data unless regulators or journalists repackage it, and the bill includes no funds for that [S2].

Small plans face real administrative burden: plans with fewer than 100 participants, many run by small employers with no benefits staff, would have to comply with the full reporting requirements for the first time [S2].

The Labor Department has one year after enactment to write the rule, and the data would only start flowing after the next plan year, so any public benefit is years away even if the bill passed quickly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost transparency measure: it creates no new benefit rules and its compliance burden falls mainly on large plans that already file annual ERISA reports, with an exemption for small claim volumes [S2]. Its main weakness is that it stops at disclosure — no penalties for high denial rates, no limits on AI denials — so its value depends on regulators, employers, and consumers actually acting on the data. As a first step toward public accountability on claim denials, the modest cost is well matched to a real information gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not acted on it, so nothing further has happened yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the Health Claim Denial Transparency Act in the House on July 16, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, whose action is the only committee step so far [S4].
No cosponsors had joined the bill as of the latest record [S3].
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote has taken place, and the bill has not moved since its referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, no one has gained or lost anything — the bill sits in committee with no cosponsors, and health plans face no new reporting duties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.role: Sponsor (GA-07), House Education and Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the committee where she sits.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors have signed on and no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is not yet visible [S3].

industries.note: Plans and their administrators would have to compile and publish detailed denial, appeal, and AI-usage data each year, exposing denial rates and reasons that are currently not publicly reported in this form. The requirement is disclosure only, so the financial hit is compliance cost plus reputational exposure rather than a direct cut to revenue [S2].

Employers bear the filing burden, especially small employers whose plans with fewer than 100 participants are newly pulled into full reporting [S2]. Employers also gain a bargaining tool: published denial data could help them shop for plans that treat claims more fairly.
Providers fight denials and appeals constantly; public denial data would support their efforts to identify and challenge plans with high denial rates. Their interest runs with patients' here.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced late in a Congress with no cosponsors rarely reach a floor vote; the realistic path is that the committee takes no action and the bill dies when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless McBath attracts cosponsors and pushes for a hearing.
